text: Given the root of a binary tree, return the length of its diameter. The diameter is the longest path between any two nodes, measured in edges. The path does not have to go through the root.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the length is counted in edges, not nodes. So a single node has diameter zero, and two nodes joined by one edge give one. Is that right?

And I want to underline the part you already said, because I think it's the whole trap in this problem. The longest path does not have to touch the root — it can sit entirely inside one subtree. So I can't just add the left height and the right height at the root and call it done. I have to consider every node as a possible turning point. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to ten to the fourth nodes, any shape.

Let me run through the example: one, two, three, four, five. Root one has children two and three, and two has children four and five. The longest path is four, two, one, three. That's three edges, so the answer is three. Here it does go through the root, but that's luck. I'll show a case later where it doesn't.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to visit every node, compute the height of its left and right sides, add them, and keep the biggest sum. That's correct, but each height call walks a whole subtree, so I pay linear time per node and land at n squared on a skewed tree. This problem reminds me of a post-order height computation with one extra job bolted on. A single post-order pass already computes every height I need, children first. So instead of asking for heights again and again, I compute each one once and grab the answer on the way back up. That turns the naive n squared into linear time, with no extra data structures.

Here's the plan. One: a helper, path, returns the height of a subtree counted in nodes — zero for empty, one for a leaf. Two: at each node, left plus right is the longest path that turns there, in edges, so I fold it into a running maximum. Three: return one plus the bigger side. One thing worth flagging — why doesn't testing left plus right at each node miss a path or count one twice? Every path has exactly one highest point, so it's owned by exactly one node, its top. Since I check every node, I cover all paths, once each. There's a trade-off here. A member variable holding the running best is a side effect; returning a pair is purer but noisier. I'll take the member and flag its risk later. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The main function guards the empty tree, runs path from the root, and returns the running best. Inside path, I get both child heights, update the best with left plus right, and return one plus the max. One thing worth flagging — the last two lines combine the same two numbers in two different ways. Left plus right is the path that turns at me: it uses both sides, so it's finished. One plus the max is the path that keeps going up through me — it can only use one side, because a path can't fork. They're not interchangeable: max on the update line fails two hundred eighty of the six hundred twenty-six trees up to seven nodes, and plus on the return line fails three hundred sixty-nine.

Let's dry-run the code with one, two, three, four, five, and I expect three. Rows are in the order the calls finish. The running best only moves twice: at node two it goes from zero to two — the path four, two, five. Then at the root, left is two and right is one, so it goes to three. The root also returns three, from one plus the max of two and one, but that agreement is a coincidence — they answer different questions. Corner cases: an empty tree returns zero from the guard. A single node has both sides zero, so the answer stays zero — no edges. And the promised one: a diameter that avoids the root needs at least six nodes, so small hand-drawn tests hide a root-only bug.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — each node is visited once with constant work. Space is order h for the call stack; in the worst-case scenario the tree is a chain, so h equals n. Oh, one more thing — longestPath is a member, and it's never reset. Run one object on one, two, three, four, five and you get three, which is right. Reuse it on one, two, whose real diameter is one, and you still get three. LeetCode hides this because it builds a fresh Solution for each test. In real code I'd reset it at the top of the main function, or pass a local by reference.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You gave a real correctness argument — every path has one highest point, so testing every node covers each path exactly once. You explained why the two adjacent lines need different operators, and what breaks when you swap them. And you noticed on your own that the un-reset member is a latent bug that LeetCode's harness happens to hide. Good work.
